dataset.what_one_row_represents: One row in birds.csv = one species recorded during one 10-minute ship-based seabird census. One row in ships.csv = one 10-minute census (a record_id) with location, weather, and observer.
dataset.geographic_scope: Tasman Sea & adjacent Southern Ocean: -69°S to -19°S, 50°E to 180°E

ana_01.label: Dataset profile: 12,310 censuses, 49,019 species rows
ana_01.content: The dataset combines 12,310 ten-minute ship-based seabird censuses (ships.csv) with 49,019 species observation rows (birds.csv). Every census has exactly one record_id and birds.record_id matches that 1-to-1 in coverage. The records span 21 years (1969-07-31 to 1990-12-21), 50 degrees of latitude (-69 to -19) and 130 degrees of longitude (50 to 180). 691 censuses (1.4%) recorded no birds at all (species_common_name is NA, originally '[NO BIRDS RECORDED]').

ana_02.label: Sparse instrument fields: 90%+ missing for depth, SST, pressure
ana_02.content: Optional instrument fields are mostly empty: depth is missing in 98.9% of censuses, sea_surface_temperature in 94.4%, atmospheric pressure in 93.7%, air_temperature in 91.6%, ship direction in 89.8%, wind_direction in 89.5%. The behavioural and minimal-meta fields, by contrast, are essentially complete (record_id, date, time, observer, latitude, longitude, hemisphere, activity, season all under 0.1% missing). Anything that an observer had to write by hand on every census got recorded; anything that needed an instrument or a separate column often did not.

ana_03.label: Top species by record count: wandering albatross dominates
ana_03.content: Among 48,328 records that recorded a species, four of the top five most-frequent log entries are wandering albatross plumage stages (PL2 with 3,104 records; PL3 with 2,885; PL1 with 1,818; PL4 with 1,475 — over 9,000 records combined). Cape petrel is second at 2,936, followed by grey-faced petrel (2,597) and prion (unidentified, 2,094). The dataset has 321 distinct log-entry strings — a long tail of identifications, sex, age, and plumage codes that all start as free text in the original log book.

ana_04.label: Top species by total birds counted: shearwaters dwarf albatrosses
ana_04.content: Ranking by sum of birds counted (excluding the six 99,999 sentinels) flips the picture: short-tailed shearwater accounts for 482,558 of the 1,342,219 birds counted across the program (36% of all birds), with prion (unidentified) at 226,500 and sooty shearwater at 174,329. Albatrosses, which dominate by record count, do not even reach the top 15 by individuals: they are seen often but in small flocks, while shearwaters are seen less often but in massive feeding aggregations of thousands.

ana_05.label: 38.7% of records cannot be resolved to a single species
ana_05.content: 18,696 of 48,328 species records (38.7%) have a scientific name containing a slash — meaning the original log entry could not be resolved to a single species and Te Papa staff recorded it as an aggregate (e.g. 'Diomedea epomophora / sanfordi / antipodensis / exulans' for the great-albatross complex). Only 29,632 records (61.3%) were identified to a single species. This is a reminder that at-sea seabird identification at speed is hard.

ana_06.label: Only 1.4% of censuses recorded zero birds
ana_06.content: Of 12,310 ten-minute censuses (one per record_id), only 691 (1.4%) recorded no birds at all — these appear in birds.csv as a single row with NA species_common_name (originally '[NO BIRDS RECORDED]'). In practice, sailing through New Zealand and Tasman Sea waters almost always meant seeing seabirds within ten minutes.

calculation.output: no-birds censuses: 691 of 49019 (1.4%)

ana_07.label: Five-year program gap (1970-1974), peak in 1987
ana_07.content: Effort is highly uneven across years. After 243 censuses in 1969 the program effectively paused — 1970 to 1974 inclusive recorded zero censuses. It restarted in 1975 (202) and ramped up through the late 1970s. The peak was 1987 with 1,634 censuses; 1984-1987 alone accounts for 5,847 of 12,310 censuses (47.5% of all program effort). Effort then crashed: 344 in 1988, 26 in 1989, 20 in 1990. The shape of this curve is a story about volunteer observer availability and ship schedules, not about bird abundance.

data_table.description: Censuses per year, 1969-1990 (zero-effort years included)

ana_08.label: Effort is roughly balanced across seasons
ana_08.content: Censuses are spread fairly evenly across the four southern-hemisphere seasons: spring 3,585, summer 3,477, autumn 2,794, winter 2,454. Spring and summer together account for 57.4% of effort — there was somewhat more activity during the warmer half of the year, but no season is missing.

ana_09.label: 98.4% of censuses are full 10-minute counts
ana_09.content: Only 199 of 12,310 censuses (1.6%) are flagged 'partial' (less than 10 minutes or casual observation); the remaining 12,111 (98.4%) are full 10-minute counts. The protocol was followed faithfully — when an observer logged a record, they almost always logged a complete count.

ana_10.label: Geographic footprint: Tasman Sea & sub-Antarctic Pacific
ana_10.content: Records span -69° to -19° latitude and 50° to 180° longitude — but the heart of the dataset is the Tasman Sea and adjacent Southern Ocean. There are far-flung points in the Indian Ocean (down to 50°E) and on the Antarctic shelf, but the bulk of effort sits between -50°S and -30°S, between 140°E and 180°E.

data_table.description: Geographic extent of the dataset

ana_11.label: 5°×5° density grid: hotspots at -40°,170° and -45°,170°
ana_11.content: Aggregating censuses into 5°×5° cells, the densest cell is centred at -40°S, 170°E with 1,293 censuses (10.5% of all program effort) and 210,861 individual birds counted; second is -45°S, 170°E with 1,104 censuses and 185,290 birds. The full grid contains 113 occupied cells. The cell with the highest bird sum, however, is -40°S, 145°E (Bass Strait area) with 230,195 birds across just 598 censuses, reflecting massive shearwater flocks rather than albatross-dominated counts. This grid powers the Tasman Sea density map.

data_table.description: Top 25 5°×5° grid cells (lat_bin/lon_bin = SW corner of cell) with census count and total birds

ana_12.label: 66% of effort lives in the -40 to -30°S band
ana_12.content: Bucketing by 10° latitude bands, 8,119 censuses (66.0% of effort) fall in -40 to -30°S — the latitudes containing the North Island and the warmer Tasman waters. The -50 to -40°S band (Subtropical Front, Subantarctic) holds 3,520 (28.6%); together these two bands capture 94.6% of all program effort. Antarctic-water records (-70 to -50°S, 590 censuses) and tropical records (-30 to -10°S, 70 censuses) are rare.

data_table.description: Censuses per 10° latitude band

ana_13.label: Behaviour incidence: a quarter of records following the ship
ana_13.content: Across 48,328 species records, the most common behaviour flags are 'following_ship' (24.5% of records, 11,819) and 'flying_past' (24.3%, 11,728). 'Accompanying' is the third (13.8%, 6,659). Active feeding is recorded in 7.5% (3,604), and 'sitting on water' in 7.2% (3,470). Rare behaviours: sitting on ice 0.1% (41), sitting on ship 0.2% (86), moulting 0.2% (83), in-hand capture 0.0% (3). About 2.0% of records (982) explicitly note natural feeding (i.e. not on ship discards).

ana_14.label: Wandering albatrosses are the dataset's #1 ship-followers
ana_14.content: Of 11,819 records flagged 'following_ship', the top followers are wandering albatross plumage stages: PL3 (1,592), PL2 (1,441), PL1 (747), PL4 (711), AD (674), and SUBAD (326) — 5,491 records, or 46.5% of all ship-following events. Other heavy followers are Cape petrel (1,021) and black-browed albatross adult (823) and unspecified (374). The ranking is dominated by exactly the species that albatross researchers describe as obligate dynamic-soarers attracted to ships and discards.

ana_16.label: Behavioural fingerprints split species into two camps
ana_16.content: Looking at the top 10 species by record count, behaviour profiles fall cleanly into two groups. Wandering albatross plumage classes follow ships in 41-55% of observations (PL3 55.2%, PL4 48.2%, PL2 46.4%, PL1 41.1%) and are almost never recorded flying past or naturally feeding. By contrast, prion (unidentified) flies past in 44.9% of records, follows ships in only 5.0%, and is the only top-10 species to actually feed naturally at any non-trivial rate (4.2%). Grey-faced petrel and Australasian gannet AD also fly past more than they follow (39.4% and 36.9% respectively). Cape petrel and black-browed albatross sit in between: meaningful following (~35% / 45%) but also visible accompanying and natural feeding.

ana_17.content: Just 26 unique observers contributed to the entire 21-year program, and one — J. Jenkins — alone accounts for 6,583 of 12,310 censuses (53.5%). The top five observers (Jenkins, N. Cheshire 1,462, A. Baines 1,250, J.D. Cleaver 1,023, M.J. Carter 747) account for 89.9% of effort; the top ten cover 96.4%. The opportunistic, volunteer-driven nature of the program means a tiny number of people produced almost all of the data.

ana_18.content: Of 12,310 censuses, 11,560 (93.9%) were taken while the ship was 'steaming, sailing'. Note that fishing and trawling — the activities most relevant to the discard-following hypothesis — are only 0.5% and 0.4% of the dataset.

ana_19.label: Wind conditions: most counts in light to moderate breezes
ana_19.content: Where wind class was logged (7,622 censuses; the rest are NA), the modal class is Beaufort 4 (moderate breeze, 11-16 kn) at 1,627 censuses. Beaufort 2-5 (light to fresh breeze) covers 5,577 of the 7,622 logged censuses (73%). True gales and above (Beaufort 8+) are rare: 217 censuses combined, with only one count each at violent storm and hurricane (and zero birds counted in the hurricane).

ana_20.label: Median count is steady from breeze to gale
ana_20.content: Median birds-per-census stays remarkably stable across the breeze range: 6 at calm, 7 at light air, 8 at Beaufort 2-4 and 6, 9 at fresh breeze, near gale, and strong gale, then 10 at gale. Mean counts are noisier because of giant flocks: 287.6 mean at Beaufort 0 (driven by a few huge static-water counts), 226.1 at Beaufort 1, dropping to 52.6-135 in the breeze range. The hurricane census (n=1) recorded zero birds. Overall, weather alone is a poor predictor of how many birds an observer recorded.

caveats.content: Six counts at the 99,999 sentinel value are excluded from total-bird sums; treating them as real numbers would massively inflate species totals.
The dataset is opportunistic effort by 26 volunteers, with 53.5% from one observer. Geographic and temporal patterns reflect ship routes and observer availability, not bird abundance.
1970-1974 contain zero censuses (program pause); the 1984-1987 peak is an effort spike, not a population spike.
38.7% of records are taxonomic aggregates (slash-separated). Species-level claims should be treated as 'log entry' rather than 'identified species'.
Wind-vs-bird-count comparisons are confounded: high winds reduce detection, and detection probability moves opposite to bird behaviour at low wind (no soaring without wind).
